He instructed the Raja to prepare a special *puja* (prayer ritual) to Devi Durga at the *ghat* (riverbank). "Offer seven *pedas* (sweets) made with pure ghee and honey to the Goddess. Only one rani, the queen with the purest heart, must offer these pedas and ask for a son."

The Raja did as he was told. He informed all seven ranis, but knowing the *choto rani's* piety, he secretly wished she would be the chosen one. The six older ranis, full of jealousy, saw their opportunity. They mixed poison into their pedas, hoping to ensure whoever ate them died and they remained the Raja’s favorite.

The *choto rani*, unaware of their wicked plan, offered her peda to Devi with true devotion. The Goddess, pleased with her pure heart, appeared in a dream and warned her, "Do not eat the peda. Take it far away and bury it in the garden."

Next morning, the choto rani, afraid and obedient, secretly buried her peda just as Devi told her to. Days turned into weeks. At the very spot, a beautiful, shimmering pomegranate tree sprouted from the ground. The tree grew laden with magnificent pomegranates, each one glowing as if lit from within.

The other ranis, consumed by jealousy, saw the tree and realized the choto rani wasn't dead. They hatched another malicious plan. They told the Raja the choto rani had planted the cursed tree herself to destroy the kingdom. They said the fruits were poisonous and asked the Raja to chop down the tree.

The Raja, heartbroken and believing their lies, ordered the tree to be felled. As the woodcutter swung his axe, the largest pomegranate burst open, and out sprang a radiant boy, his eyes filled with the wisdom of ages. He pleaded, “Baba (Father) do not kill me! I am Dalim Kumar, your son!”

The Raja, stunned, embraced his son. The choto rani, hearing the commotion, ran outside and fainted with joy at the sight of her son.

The wicked ranis, seeing their treachery revealed, panicked. They cursed the boy, saying, "He will turn into a stone every night and only turn back into a boy with the touch of his mother's tears."

Sure enough, every night, Dalim Kumar turned into a stone murti (statue). The choto rani wept every single night, her tears falling on the cold stone until Daalim Kumar turned back into an alive, beautiful boy every dawn.

The six older ranis, seeing the success of their curse, were even more furious. This time they bribed the Raja's minister, the *deowan*, to take Dalim Kumar away. They paid him to take Dalim Kumar deep into the forest and leave him there, to be devoured by tigers and wolves.

The loyal deowan however realized the evil of the other ranis and couldn't kill the boy. Instead he took Dalim Kumar to a village and left him with a poor Brahmin family, telling them the Raja himself had sent the boy to be cared for.

Dalim Kumar grew up with the Brahmin family, strong and wise. One day, while tending cows he heard of a beautiful princess who was mute. Every Raja and prince in the world had tried to make her speak, but none had succeeded.

Dalim Kumar, with nothing to lose, decided to try his luck. He travelled to the kingdom with his newfound fortune and asked to try to make the princess speak. At first, the Raja refused, but was so impressed by Dalim Kumar's beauty that he eventually agreed.

Dalim Kumar sat near the princess and played a melodious tune on his bansuri (flute), a raga (musical mode) filled with the music of Bengal’s rivers and fields. He sang a song about a cursed boy, a jealous queen, and a mother’s love. The princess, hearing the tale, was moved to tears. She cried out, "He is Dalim Kumar! He is the rightful heir!"

The Raja, overjoyed that his daughter could speak, immediately agreed to have her marry Dalim Kumar. Word traveled to the old Raja who immediately came to the kingdom with his choto rani and repented with full heart.

Dalim Kumar reunited with his parents, punished the wicked ranis and ruled justly as a wise and benevolent Raja. He loved his rani and was a good son, honoring his foster parents and all who had helped him along the way.

And so, that is the story of Dalim Kumar, born of a pomegranate and the unwavering love of a pure-hearted mother. Joi Maa Durga! (Victory to Mother Durga!)

Alright, let's retell the story of Kolavati Rajkonna (কলবতী রাজকন্যা), the Banana Blossom Princess, from Dakshinaranjan Mitra Majumdar’s Thakurmar Jhuli, trying to preserve its cultural nuances and kinship terms.

The story begins in a kingdom, long ago, where lived a Raja (King) and his Rani (Queen). They were blessed with six sons, all brave and accomplished. Yet, their hearts ached for a daughter. They prayed to the gods night and day, offering puja (worship) and dan-dakshina (charity) to the brahmins. Finally, Bhagoban (God) heard their pleas. A divine voice instructed the Raja, "Do not despair. You will find your daughter within a Kalagach (banana plant)."

Overjoyed, the Raja searched his entire kingdom until he found a Kalagach in his own bari (compound) which was unlike any other. It shimmered with an otherworldly glow. He, along with the Rani and the six Rajkumars (Princes), gathered around the Kalagach. With trembling hands, the Raja ordered his most trusted servants to carefully slice open the kola (banana) flower, the shimmering kolaboti.

And lo! From the heart of the kolaboti emerged a beautiful baby girl, radiant as the morning sun. Their prayers answered, the Raja and Rani named her Kolavati Rajkonna, the Banana Blossom Princess. The entire palace echoed with joyous uludhvani (a high-pitched, tremulous sound made by women during auspicious occasions) and sankha sounds (blowing of conch shells).

Kolavati Rajkonna grew up surrounded by love and luxury. Her six brothers doted on her, buying her the finest silks from Banaras and the sweetest sandesh (Bengali sweets). They were fiercely protective of their only sister.

Now, the time came for the Rajkumars to marry. The Raja organized a swayamvara (a ceremony where the princess chooses her husband from a group of suitors) for each of his six sons. Each Rakjumar, one after the other, went to distant lands and bought beautiful brides and with a pomp and fanfare, brought them to the Rajbari(king's palace).

The six new boudis (sister-in-laws) were jealous of Kolavati’s beauty and the love she received from her brothers. The seeds of jealousy began to sprout in their hearts like weeds. They secretly poisoned the minds of their respective husbands, whispering that Kolavati was pampered and lazy, contributing nothing to the family.

One day, the eldest bou (wife of the eldest prince), driven by spite, suggested a test. “Dada (elder brother), let Kolavati prove her worth. Let her make the finest pithas (rice cakes) for the upcoming Durga Puja!” The other boudis chimed in agreement, their eyes gleaming with malice.

Kolavati, though saddened by their coldness, accepted the challenge. She went to the kitchen and, with great devotion and skill, began to prepare the pithas. She ground the rice flour, grated the coconut, and mixed in jaggery with the best of her ability. But as she was cooking, the boudis, with evil intentions, threw a handful of ash into the batter.

Kolavati, unaware of their treachery, continued to cook. When the pithas were ready, they were, of course, horrible. Bitter and gritty, they were inedible. The boudis spread rumors throughout the Rajbari, declaring Kolavati incapable and worthless. She was now a target for ridicule.

Heartbroken and humiliated, Kolavati retreated to her room, tears streaming down her face. One night, overwhelmed by despair, she decided to leave the palace. She packed a small bundle of clothes and a few silver coins. Under the veil of darkness, she slipped out of the Rajbari, leaving behind everything she had ever known.

She wandered through forests and fields, her feet sore and her heart heavy. Finally, she came to a dense jungle and found a small, dilapidated hut. Taking shelter within, she fell asleep, exhausted.

The next morning, she woke up to the sound of birdsong. She noticed a gach (tree) laden with plump berries. She picked and ate them, her hunger momentarily appeased. Resolving to survive, she decided to gather firewood and try to sell it in a nearby gram (village).

She worked tirelessly, collecting wood and carrying it to the gram. Slowly, she began to earn a meager living. She bought food and clothes, but never forgot her former life of luxury. She lived simply, always maintaining her dignity and grace.

One day, while selling firewood in the gram, she encountered a wealthy merchant, a shaudagor (merchant). Impressed by her beauty, her gentle nature, and her hard work, he fell in love with her. He proposed marriage, promising her a life of comfort and happiness.

Kolavati, though hesitant at first, saw the sincerity in his eyes. She confided in him about her past, her royal lineage, and the injustice she had suffered. The shaudagor, far from being deterred, vowed to avenge her. They were married with great pomp and ceremony, and Kolavati became the shaudagor’s wife.

Now, the shaudagor, being a shrewd businessman, devised a plan. He began trading with the kingdom of Kolavati's father. He deliberately bought and sold goods at a loss, creating a situation where the Raja's treasury was dwindling rapidly.

Hearing of this economic crisis, the Raja called a meeting of his ministers. He lamented his misfortune, wondering how to save his kingdom from ruin. The shaudagor, posing as a loyal merchant, offered his services. "Maharaj (Your Majesty)," he said, "I can save your kingdom, but I have one condition."

The Raja, desperate for help, agreed to any condition. The shaudagor then revealed his true intention: "I will only help if your six boudis cook a feast for me and my wife."

The Raja, though puzzled, agreed. He summoned his six boudis and instructed them to prepare a lavish feast for the shaudagor and his wife. The boudis, arrogant and confident, readily accepted the challenge.

As the boudis bustled about the kitchen, preparing the feast, the shaudagor and his wife arrived at the palace. The Raja greeted them with honor and led them to the dining hall. The boudis, eager to impress, presented their dishes with pride.

But as the shaudagor and his wife tasted the food, they began to choke and cough. The dishes were bland, burnt, over-salted, and utterly inedible. The Raja was horrified. He demanded to know what was wrong.

Then, the shaudagor's wife, Kolavati, stepped forward. With tears streaming down her face, she revealed her true identity. "I am Kolavati Rajkonna, the daughter you abandoned because of these wicked women! They threw ash in my pitha batter, causing me to flee my home!"

The Raja was stunned. He looked at his boudis, their faces pale with fear and guilt. The truth was revealed. Their jealousy, their treachery, their cruelty, all stood bare for everyone to see.

The Raja was filled with remorse. He banished his boudis from the kingdom, showering them with scorn. He begged Kolavati for forgiveness. Kolavati, though hurt, forgave her father and her brothers. She returned to the Rajbari, not as a pampered princess, but as a wise and respected woman.

The shaudagor helped restore the kingdom's wealth. Kolavati ruled alongside her brothers, advising them with her wisdom and compassion. The kingdom prospered under her guidance, and the story of Kolavati Rajkonna, the Banana Blossom Princess who overcame adversity, became a beloved folktale told and retold in the villages of Bengal, a timeless reminder of the power of resilience, forgiveness, and the ultimate triumph of good over evil.  The story is a popular one retold for generations in every bengali household, especially to the grandchildren by their 'thakuma' (grandmother).

Alright, let's delve into the magical world of Thakurmar Jhuli and retell the tale of Shat Bhai Champa, preserving its Bengali essence.

**The Story of Shat Bhai Champa (Seven Brothers Champa)**

Once upon a time, in a kingdom draped in silks and scented with sandalwood, lived a king deeply devoted to his seven queens. But alas, none bore him a son. Discouraged, he finally married a humble woman, Rani Durba, known for her kindness and gentle heart.

Soon, Rani Durba’s belly swelled with promise. The other queens, devoured by jealousy ( *rishiri bhare dushho bhare* ), plotted her downfall. They whispered venom in the king’s ear, claiming she was not with child at all, but only faking. Sadly, the king, weakened by their constant accusations, started doubting his Rani's pure heart.

As the time drew near, Rani Durba, unaware of the treachery brewing, was secretly helped by her faithful *dai ma* (midwife). On a dark, stormy night, she gave birth to not one, not two, but seven beautiful sons! The *dai ma*, overjoyed, carefully bundled the *saptaputro* (seven sons) to show to the king.

But the jealous queens intercepted the *dai ma*. Cruelly, they stole the seven *narashishu* (newborn boys) and replaced them with seven puppies. Horrified, the *dai ma* could only weep silently as they then presented the puppies to the despairing king. The scheming queens then buried the seven innocent princes alive in the *upaban* (royal garden), under a flourishing champak tree.

Rani Durba was devastated. Forced to present her “offspring” to the King and witnessing his disappointment, she was branded a fraud and banished to the *ghordaal* (stable), forced to live a life of shame and servitude. She spent her days sweeping and tending to the horses, her heart heavy with an unspoken sorrow.

Meanwhile, in the *upaban*, a miracle occurred. From the earth, rose seven beautiful champak buds, one for each prince. Every morning, Rani Durba, forced to clean the stables beside the *upaban*, noticed the magnificent *champa* blossoms. She felt inexplicably drawn to them, unable to understand the depth of her connection with them. She'd caress the delicate petals, and whisper soft lullabies, *“Aai, aai chonda, mama tor kotha…*”, the same songs she would have sung to her babies.

One day, a *sadhu baba* (holy man) passed through the kingdom. He sat under the champak tree to meditate. He instantly recognized the unusual energy emanating from the blossoms.  He observed Rani Durba’s daily visits and her deep affection for the flowers.  Intuition told him something was amiss. He called for her and gently questioned her, sensing her hidden grief. Rani Durba, after much hesitation, confided her tragic story to the revered *sadhu baba*.

The *sadhu baba* listened intently, his eyes filled with compassion. He instructed Rani Durba to perform a special *puja* (prayer ritual). He procured seven small clay bowls and told her to fill them with *amrito jol* (ambrosial water) and to smear the base of the *champa* tree with *alta* (red dye, traditionally used by women).

Following the *sadhu baba's* instructions to the letter, Rani Durba performed the *puja*. As she poured the *amrito jol* and painted the tree with *alta*, she chanted, " *Sat Bhai Champa, keu ki acho? Tumi ki amar putra ho?* (Seven Brothers Champa, is anyone there? Are you my sons?)"

Miraculously, as the last drop of water touched the ground, the seven *champa* buds transformed into seven beautiful princes!  Dressed in radiant robes, they embraced their mother, their tears of joy mixing with her own.

The truth quickly unraveled. Word reached the king who, upon hearing the *sadhu baba’s* testimony and witnessing the miraculous transformation, realized the extent of his queens’ treachery.  Filled with remorse, he rescued Rani Durba from the *ghordaal*, adorned her in jewels, and welcomed her back to the palace with immense respect. The guilty queens were punished justly (usually exiled or worse, depending on the telling), and Rani Durba and her seven sons brought prosperity and joy to the kingdom. The boys, known as Shat Bhai Champa, grew up to be wise and valiant princes, always cherishing the memory of their early struggle and their mother's enduring love. They understood that the power of love can overcome the darkest treachery and turn even flowers back into princes.

**Cultural Nuances Preserved:**

*   **Kinship Terms:** The relationships are carefully defined using terms like *dai ma* (midwife), *rani* (queen), *narashishu* (newborn child), *saptaputro* (seven sons), *sadhu baba* (holy man).
*   **Rituals:** The significance of *puja*, *amrito jol* (ambrosial water), and *alta* (red dye) are maintained, reflecting their role in Bengali cultural practices. The lullaby *"Aai, aai chonda, mama tor kotha…"*, embodies a mother's love and connection to her child.
*   **Themes:** Emphasis on the destructive power of jealousy (*rishiri bhare dushho bhare*), the importance of unwavering maternal love, and the triumph of good over evil.
*   **Setting:** The story is situated in a traditional Bengali kingdom with specific locations like the *upaban* (royal garden) and *ghordaal* (stable) mentioned.
*   **Language:** Certain phrases, like the chant "*Sat Bhai Champa, keu ki acho? Tumi ki amar putra ho?* ", are used to retain the authentic Bengali flavor.

This retelling aims to capture the essence of the original folktale, maintaining its cultural context and emotional depth. The specific details may vary slightly depending on the version from Thakurmar Jhuli, as with all oral traditions. However, the core narrative and its underlying themes remain consistent, offering a glimpse into the rich storytelling heritage of Bengal.

Alright, let's dust off the pages of Thakurmar Jhuli and revisit the crafty tale of Sheyal Pandit (Fox Scholar). Imagine, now, sitting on a verandah bathed in the golden light of dusk, listening to Thakurma (Grandmother) narrate this familiar story:

"Anek anek din ager kotha. One upon a time, in a distant land, there lived a crafty Sheyal Pandit. He thought himself very clever, you see, a veritable 'bou-bhat-e achcha' (good at feasts). But his cleverness was mostly borrowed, a mask for pure laziness and greed.

Now, near a bustling village, there lived a hardworking peasant, a Chasha Bhai (Brother Farmer). The Chasha Bhai, with the sweat of his brow, tilled his fields, growing luscious pumpkins, kumuRo. He would load them onto his bullock cart, carefully arranged like precious jewels, and take them to the haat (market) to sell.

One day, Sheyal Pandit, stomach rumbling louder than a monsoon thunder, spied the Chasha Bhai's cart laden with kumuRo. His eyes gleamed like chana bhaja (fried chickpeas) under the sun. 'Ah,' he thought, 'opportunity knocks!'

He raced ahead and, finding a narrow part of the path, lay down, feigning death. He stiffened his legs, lolled his tongue out, and closed his eyes. He looked, truly, quite gone to meet his ancestors!

The Chasha Bhai, driving his bullocks slowly, noticed the seemingly lifeless Sheyal. 'Ram Ram!' he exclaimed, crossing himself. 'Ei ki holo? What happened? Poor creature!' He stopped his cart and, with a heavy heart, poked Sheyal Pandit with his Lathi (stick). No movement.

'Shotti korei toh more geche (Truly, he's dead)!' he sighed. The Chasha Bhai, being a pious and kind soul, thought it a sin to leave a creature unburied. He knew the proper rite for an animal death involved burial under a Neem tree, a sacred spot cleansing of earthly sins.

Thinking to give the Sheyal a proper 'antim sanskar' (final rites), he carefully picked up the seemingly lifeless creature and placed him on top of the kumuRo, amongst his precious pumpkins. 'Jaak, punno hobey (Well, I'll gain merit),' he muttered. Then, he continued on his way, humming a tune.

Now, Sheyal Pandit, as soon as the Chasha Bhai turned his back, sprang to life! He was heavier than he had anticipated! He quickly rolled off the largest, juiciest kumuRo, biting into it with gusto. 'Aha! Bhari mishti (So sweet)!' He devoured a considerable portion, throwing the rind aside. This continued all the way to the haat. He feasted like a Raja (king) riding in his palanquin!

Finally, the Chasha Bhai arrived at the haat. Eagerly, he began to unload his pumpkins. One by one, he lifted them down, surprised to find each a little lighter than he remembered. Then, he reached the bottom of the pile.

'O ma go!' He exclaimed. The biggest pumpkin was half-eaten, with muddy paw prints all over it! He instantly understood. 'Sheyal er chhal! (The fox's trick!)' he cried.

Enraged but also somewhat amused, he hatched a plan. He sold the remaining kumuRo for a good price, then bought a large, empty Dhol (drum). He placed it strategically near a tree, just outside the village.

That evening, Sheyal Pandit, stomach full of pumpkin and swaggering with self-importance, sauntered past the tree. He heard the faint sound of music emanating from the Dhol. Curiosity, a trait that often accompanies foolishness, got the better of him.

'Ki re baba? (What's going on?)' He inquired, peering inside. He saw the reflection of his own cunning face staring back at him. Thinking it was another Sheyal, a challenger maybe, he puffed out his chest and roared, 'Ke re tui? Who are you? Come out and fight!'

Of course, only his own echo answered him. He roared again, even louder. Still nothing.

Frustrated, he jumped inside the Dhol, determined to confront this 'challenger'. Now, the Chasha Bhai, who had been hiding nearby, quickly clamped the lid shut and secured it tight.

Locked inside the Dhol, Sheyal Pandit realized his folly. Panic set in. He banged and screamed, but it was no use.

The Chasha Bhai, chuckling to himself, took the Dhol to the Dhobi ghat (washerman's place) by the river. He bribed the Dhobi Dada (Brother Washerman) with a piece of gud (jaggery) and instructed him to give the Dhol a thorough beating all day.

All day long, the Dhobi Dada pounded the Dhol with his bat, the rhythmic ‘dhuk dhuk’ echoing through the village. Inside, Sheyal Pandit was getting the beating of his life!

By evening, when the Chasha Bhai returned, the cries of the Sheyal had subsided to feeble whimpers. The Dhobi Dada, his arms aching, handed over the Dhol.

The Chasha Bhai opened the lid and out crawled a thoroughly bruised and humbled Sheyal Pandit. He was no longer the swaggering 'bou-bhat-e achcha', but a sorry sight, whimpering and covered in dust.

'Ebar bujhli? (Now you understand?)' the Chasha Bhai said, sternly. 'Laziness and dishonesty never prosper. Go and earn your own living honestly!'

Sheyal Pandit, completely defeated, limped away into the jungle, never again to trouble the Chasha Bhai, or anyone else in the village, with his cunning tricks.

And that, my dear granddaughter, is the story of Sheyal Pandit. Remember, cleverness without honesty is like a boat without a rudder – it will eventually sink!"

Thakurma would then pat your head, her face crinkled with a knowing smile. The air would be filled with the scent of burning incense sticks and the distant calls of jackals, a reminder that even in the deepest jungle, honesty and hard work are always the best path.

story_name: marriage with the prince of snake_EN_3
retelling:
Chandrabati, a beautiful maiden, was renowned for her piety and devotion to the goddess Manasa. One day, while offering prayers, she discovered a snake prince, injured and seemingly lifeless. Her compassion overwhelmed her, leading her to nurse him back to health. Unknown to her, the snake prince, Chandradhar, was deeply moved by her kindness and fell in love. He eventually revealed his true form and proposed marriage.

Chandrabati, torn between societal expectations and her own feelings, hesitated. Snakes were considered inauspicious, and marriage to one was unheard of. Her fear of societal judgment and what it would bring was great. However, Chandradhar pleaded, emphasizing his genuine love and devotion. Witnessing his sincerity, Chandrabati chose love and compassion over societal norms, agreeing to marry him.

The folktale imparts the importance of compassion, empathy, and judging others based on their character rather than outward appearances or societal prejudices. Chandrabati teaches us to challenge preconceived notions and prioritize genuine love and intention while showing the importance of the strength to act on it.

story_name: the consequence of a broken promise_EN_3
retelling:
Once in a Bengal village, lived a woodcutter named Ram, known for his honeyed words but weak promises. He vowed to offer the first fruit of his mango tree to the village deity, but when luscious mangoes grew, greed overpowered him. He ate them all, forgetting his promise.

Soon after, Ram fell terribly ill. No medicine worked. An old woman, wise in the ways of the village, recognized the curse of a broken vow. She advised Ram to recreate the mango grove in miniature, entirely from sugar, and offer it to the deity, truly repenting his deceit.

Ram, humbled and weak, painstakingly sculpted the sugar grove, pouring his remorse into each sugary mango. He offered it to the deity with tears in his eyes. Slowly, his health recovered.

The tale teaches that reneging on a promise, especially one made to a higher power or community, breeds consequences. It emphasizes the importance of honesty and integrity. While tempting to prioritize immediate desires, the story reminds us that actions have repercussions, and true repentance and restitution can often heal the breach created by broken trust. It warns against the dangers of greed and the enduring power of keeping one's word.

A wealthy, dying merchant had accumulated his riches through deceit. Knowing death was near, he summoned two witnesses: a poor barber and a powerful king, and entrusted them to divide his massive fortune equally between his two feuding sons. After he died, the king, consumed by greed, influenced the barber to lie, awarding the elder son almost everything.

The younger son, destitute, wandered disconsolate. He built a pyre to end his life, but before lighting it, he threw rice into a nearby pond, creating bubbles. A wise old woman, witnessing this, inquired. He explained his plight. She instructed him to summon the king and barber back to the pond, claiming the bubbles, 'morar shakkhi', witnessed his father's will.

The king, terrified and superstitious, confessed his deception. The barber, overwhelmed by guilt, corroborated. Thus, the bubbles restored justice, righting the wrong done.

The tale teaches the virtues of honesty and integrity, contrasting them with the destructive power of greed and deceit. It also highlights the existence of a higher power, represented by the bubbles, capable of exposing wickedness and restoring balance when earthly justice fails. Ultimately, it underscores the importance of righteousness and the inevitable consequences of corruption.

story_name: Fifteen Sizzles, Three to Eat, The She-goat's Sign Is By The Binna Tree_EN_3
retelling:
A poor woodcutter and his wife were blessed with endless gold flowing from their backyard. But, they became greedy, obsessively wanting more. A wandering fakir, knowing of their fortune, asked for shelter. The woodcutter, unwilling to share his wealth, gruffly offered him a cold hearth and a meager dinner.

The fakir, discerning their avarice, uttered a riddle: "Fifteen sizzles, three to eat, The She-goat's sign is by the Binna tree." He then disappeared. Overjoyed, the woodcutter and his wife obsessed over the riddle, convinced it led to even *more* gold. They chased every possible interpretation, ignoring their existing bounty.

Eventually, the woodcutter’s wife remembered their goat often sheltered beneath the Binna tree. They dug frantically, finding nothing but disappointment. Their greed-fueled obsession drained them, souring their days. Meanwhile, their initial stream of gold mysteriously ceased. The fakir's riddle, meant to test them, revealed their corrupted hearts. The lesson: contentment is true wealth. Greed blinds us to what we already possess, leading to unhappiness and ultimately, loss. The riddle ultimately highlights that true riches aren't always measured in gold, but in gratitude and generosity.

Noshi and Dimshi, two lazy sisters, were tasked with bringing vegetables to market. En route, they encountered a playful monkey who offered to transport the basket in exchange for a share of the profits. Greedy, the sisters agreed, believing the monkey would scare away buyers, leaving all proceeds to them.

The monkey, however, proved a shrewd trader. His entertaining antics drew crowds, and the vegetables sold out for a high price. Noshi and Dimshi, expecting to cheat the monkey, were stunned when he demanded his fair share. They tried to trick him, offering him the inferior vegetables.

Wise to their deception, the monkey scattered the remaining vegetables, showing how little he valued their dishonesty. He then disappeared into the forest, leaving the sisters empty-handed and filled with shame.

The tale teaches that greed and laziness lead to ruin. Honesty and hard work are more rewarding than trying to deceive others. Furthermore, it warns against underestimating those who appear different or less intelligent, as they may possess a wisdom that surpasses our own.

A greedy and proud Brahmin, obsessed with fame, undertook a dangerous journey to collect a magical mushroom named 'Khumpui' believed to grant immense knowledge. Despite warnings, he sneered at the simple villagers, relying on his intellect alone. He found the elusive fungus deep in a perilous forest, guarded by spirits.

His arrogance made him disobey the spirits' instructions: to cook and eat the Khumpui immediately, alone and in silence. He planned to share it with royalty, hoping to gain even greater renown. Delighted with his perceived cleverness, he carried the mushroom back.

However, on his return, Khumpui began to decompose, its power fading. By the time he reached the court, it was useless, and the Brahmin was left empty-handed and humiliated. He learned a harsh lesson: pride comes before a fall, and ignoring the wisdom of those who possess local knowledge leads to failure. Khumpui teaches us the value of humility, respecting tradition, and appreciating the present rather than chasing future glory. It's a tale about listening to seasoned voices and understanding that knowledge is not always meant to be hoarded or exploited for personal gain.

Once upon a time, a king's youngest son, Dalim Kumar, was thrown into the jungle out of jealousy by his wicked sisters-in-law. Saved by a kind old woman, Dalim grows into a strong and handsome prince. He discovers a magical flute; its music creates anything he desires.

Using the flute, Dalim builds a magnificent palace and marries a beautiful princess, bringing her to live with him. News of Dalim's wealth and happiness reaches his family. Driven by greed, his sisters-in-law visit, pretending to be remorseful. They trick Dalim into revealing the flute's secret and steal it while he sleeps.

Dalim, now impoverished, is heartbroken but remembers his grandmother's advice: perseverance leads to success. He sets off on a long and arduous journey until he reaches his sisters-in-law’s kingdom. There, he cleverly recovers the flute, reminding them of their deceit and karma. Returning to his kingdom, Dalim punishes his sisters-in-law and lives happily ever after with his queen.

The tale emphasizes the importance of **honesty**, **perseverance**, and **karma**. While jealousy and greed can lead to temporary gains, they ultimately result in suffering. Dalim's ultimate victory embodies the idea that hard work and moral integrity will always triumph over deceit and malice.

Once upon a time, a poor farmer found a beautiful girl inside a banana flower, naming her Kolaboti Rajkonna. Her beauty attracted the greedy king, who planned to marry her. However, Kolaboti, wise and compassionate, knew the king's intentions were selfish. She set him impossible tasks: finding a single rice grain to feed all his kingdom and creating a magical thread that could weave itself.

The king, unable to fulfill her demands, became enraged and imprisoned her. But Kolaboti never lost hope. She used her kindness and intelligence to gain the respect of her guards and the villagers, inspiring them to challenge the king's unjust rule. Eventually, the villagers, emboldened by Kolaboti's spirit, rose up and deposed the king. Kolaboti, choosing service over power, became a beloved advisor to the new, just rulers, always advocating for the poor and vulnerable.

'Kolaboti Rajkonna' teaches that true beauty resides not just in appearance but also in kindness and wisdom. It champions the power of intelligence and compassion in overcoming adversity and challenging injustice. It also suggests that true leadership lies not in power and control, but in service to others and fighting for what is right.

Queen Lalana and Queen Kamalini, though married to the same king, were drastically different in fortune. Lalana, blessed with ten sons, was envied by the childless Kamalini. Jealousy festered, and Kamalini, fueled by a wicked maid, plotted against Lalana. Each time Lalana gave birth, Kamalini replaced the babies with puppies and had them buried alive.

But fate intervened. From beneath the soil, ten Champa saplings sprouted, transforming each day into ten beautiful boys, known as 'Shat Bhai Champa' (Seven Brothers Champa). A wise old woman, privy to their secret, prophesied their eventual reunion with their mother.

Years later, a magical river transported the ten brothers to the king's court where their beautiful singing and demeanor charmed everyone. When the king heard their melodious song about their true mother’s suffering, he saw through Kamalini's deceit.

Kamalini was punished, and Lalana was reunited with her long-lost sons. The tale teaches the dangers of jealousy and the power of truth. It also highlights the unwavering bonds of family and the eventual triumph of good over evil, even when faced with cruelty and injustice. It reinforces the belief that truth will always prevail and bring justice.

Sheyal Pondit, the clever fox, boasted of his wisdom to a tiger. The tiger, impressed, asked Sheyal to teach him. Sheyal agreed, but fearing the tiger's strength, devised a plan.

He led the tiger to a farmer's field where they were seemingly stuck to a buffalo scarecrow tied with rope. Sheyal claimed it was a test of strength and intelligence. He then 'freed' himself by feigning strain and cleverly untying his rope, leaving the tiger bound.

The farmer, seeing the tiger trapped, thrashed him mercilessly. Sheyal, watching from afar, laughed. The tiger, finally free, understood Sheyal's deception and vowed revenge.

The moral of the story is two-fold. Firstly, it highlights the dangers of boasting and being easily flattered. The tiger's vanity blinded him, making him vulnerable to Sheyal's trickery. Secondly, it demonstrates the importance of real wisdom over superficial intelligence. While Sheyal was clever, his deceitful actions ultimately revealed his lack of genuine understanding of respect and honesty, illustrating that true strength lies not just in power but in integrity. Relying solely on cunning can backfire.

story_name: marriage with the prince of snake_EN_4
retelling: In a country long ago, a couple lived with their beautiful daughter, Bilkis Banu. The father died, leaving Bilkis and her greedy mother, Sona Banu, alone in a house near a jungle. One cold morning, a python, driven by hunger, sought warmth in their courtyard. Sona Banu, mistaking the inert python for a disguised prince, decided to marry Bilkis to it. She dressed Bilkis and sent her outside, where the python began to swallow her. As Bilkis screamed each swallowed feet/waist/hands/neck/ears/head was hurting her, Sona Banu soothed her daughter said the snake was only putting anklets/waist chain/bangles/necklace/earrings/head ornament on her. After completely devouring Bilkis, the python digested her and left before dawn, leaving behind only her clothes. Sona Banu finally realized her mistake and mourned Bilkis' death. Alone, she abandoned her home and sought refuge in a distant village.

story_name: the consequence of a broken promise_EN_4
retelling:
At the joining of the Mathabhanga river, it was typical for passing cargo ships to give a portion of their goods to the local goddess. One time, a merchant refused to give anything and insulted the goddess. As a result, his boat sank into the river.

People tried to find the bottom of the river with long ropes, but they could not reach it. A brave man then volunteered to dive. Underwater, he saw a golden boat and two fairies who were pulling on the rope used to find him. He pleaded for his boat back, and the fairies agreed, saying he’d find it at the Kazis' ghat, but warned him not to tell anyone what he had seen or he would die.

The boat was found where the fairies said it would be. However, the man couldn't keep silent and told his wife what had occurred. He then vomited blood and died, as the fairies had foretold.

A man committed murder and buried the body near his home. Years passed, and the crime remained unsolved, fading from memory. One rainy day, the man, while stripping jute, noticed bubbles rising from the ground where he buried the body. Amused that his sin remained undiscovered, he smiled. His wife noticed and repeatedly questioned him. Eventually, he confessed to killing [Name] and burying him in that spot, boasting about how he had evaded justice. Later, the man and his wife had a fierce argument. In anger, she revealed his crime, and the news spread quickly. The victim's relatives informed the police, who arrested the man. He was ultimately punished for his crime.

story_name: Fifteen Sizzles, Three to Eat, The She-goat's Sign Is By The Binna Tree_EN_4
retelling: A couple argued while the wife made pithas. The husband counted fifteen sizzling sounds as she cooked. She served him three pithas, and he remarked, "Fifteen sizzles, three to eat." The wife, surprised he knew the count, believed he was a fortune-teller. She told the neighbors, and a woman who lost her goat asked him to use his powers. Annoyed, the husband told her to return later. He searched for the goat and found it near a binna tree. When the woman returned, he said, "Fifteen sizzles, three to eat, the she-goat's sign is by the binna tree." The woman found her goat there. The man then became known as Gonok Thakur, the Revered Fortune-teller.

Nasi and Dimsi were walking down a deserted road when they heard a voice offering marriage. They ignored it at first, but the voice persisted. Eventually, they discovered it was a monkey jumping in the trees and tempting them with gifts if they married him.

They reached a wide canal they couldn't cross. Desperate, they promised to marry the monkey if he helped them. He agreed, carried them across one by one, but after reaching the other side they broke their promise.

The monkey followed, undeterred. The sisters then saw a woodpecker nest and told the monkey if he got them the baby birds, they would marry him. He agreed and climbed the tree but trapped his hand in the nest. He was dividing the chicks up for each sister. Impatient, the sisters grew annoyed and threatened to leave. In a panic, trying to get free, the monkey pulled so hard that his arm ripped off and he fell into thick mud, trapping him.

In a village called Naran, lived Darbasing, a busy priest, and his two daughters, Khumpuiti and Khumbarti. While Khumbarti was known for her beauty, both sisters worked hard in their Jhum fields, enduring tough conditions to cultivate crops. One day, Khumpuiti, overwhelmed by their struggles and seeking help, wished for assistance, even from an animal. A multi-colored snake then appeared, transforming into a man who offered to help with the Jhum work under the condition that Khumpuiti never reveal his true form and feed him rice daily.

The snake helped build a Jhum hut, cleared the field, and built bird-scarers to protect their crops. Meanwhile, Khumpuiti's health declined as she shared her rice with the snake. Her father noticed her declining health and questioned Khumbarti for the reason. After initial hesitations, Khumbarti revealed her sister's pact with the snake. Darbasing, fearing the snake and its drain on his daughter, plotted to kill it. He tricked Khumbarti into luring the snake with a feast. When the snake arrived, Darbasing ambushed and killed it with a sword.

Heartbroken, Khumbarti collected the severed pieces of the snake and placed them in places her elder sister frequented. Upon discovering the fate of her snake-husband, Khumpuiti, in deep sorrow, strung the pieces into a garland and drowned herself in the river, but before doing so, she instructed her younger sister to wait for the king's hunters at the Crossroads and follow their instructions.

Following her sister's final advice, Khumbarti reached the banyan and sat on one of its branches. True to her sister's vision, the hunters spotted her and notified the king. The king arrived, charmed by her beauty, and made her his queen. The king soon had a child, during her pregnancy the old queens hatched a plan to make Khumbarti look as if she gave birth to puppies and kittens by throwing the babies into the river and replacing them at birth. The king banished the youngest queen, Khumbarti, by the riverside to herd ducks.

Local people kept hearing a lullaby by the shore. The lullaby mentioned the babies wanted a mother who would relieve Khumbarti's hardship, herding ducks. People spread the word about the babies who appeared and disappeared. The king had all the fishermen cast nets, but no one caught the babies.

One day, after growing old enough, the seven children from the river talked to their aunt Khumpuriti, who told them what had happened to their mother and that their task was to go to the banyan where the hunters were and, just like their mother, answer that they are mortal. But that they could only reveal the identity of their mother if and only if the woman could stand on the ground, squeeze her breast, and make seven streams of milk reach their mouths.

This again, true to prophecy, happened just like that, and the king was once again notified and was there himself to witness it. The queen proved she was their mother and was once again held as one of the family and the six original queens cast out.
A king, queen, and prince lived in a palace. The queen's life was tied to a pair of dice,

Once upon a time, a king with seven queens – the Eldest, Second, Third, Fourth, Fifth, Unfavored, and Youngest - was unhappy because none had given him a child.

A hermit gave the Eldest Queen a root, promising beautiful sons if they shared it. The queens agreed to share, with each preparing a portion of the meal. At the kitchen, the Eldest, Second, Third, Fifth, and Unfavored Queen did tasks; the Fourth drew water; the Youngest cleaned fish near an ash heap. The Eldest Queen had the Unfavored Queen grind the root. The Unfavored ate a piece, then gave its paste to the Eldest Queen. The Eldest Queen ate some then passed it around, with each other queen taking a portion– the Fourth Queen found only a tiny bit. The Youngest Queen received nothing and fainted as a result. The other queens blamed each other. The fourth queen suggested the youngest queen try drinking water runoff from the grinding stone. The others agreed mockingly.

Ten months and ten days later, the Eldest, Second, Third and Fifth queens each gave birth to beautiful sons. (Hira, Manik, Moti, Shankha, and Kanchan) To the shame of the Fourth Queen she had an owl (Bhutum), and the Youngest, a monkey (Buddhu). The kingdom rejoiced at the birth of 5 royal heirs, and mourned that of the unfortunate owl and monkey.

The Fourth and Youngest Queens were shunned, becoming a maid in the menagerie and a servant collecting dung cakes.

As the princes and their sons grew, the five princes behaved badly and caused general distress. As children, Bhutum and Buddhu played on the bakul tree outside of their mother's hut. Bhutum fed birds and Buddhu brought fruits to their mothers in the forest and lived humble lives.

One day, the princes found Bhutum and Buddhu. They were captured for pets, and taken to the palace.The menagerie maid and dung-cake-collecting servant mothers were devastated. Discovering their mothers' identities, the princes cast Bhutum and Buddhu out. Bhutum and Buddhu realized they are also king’s sons!

The princes left on Mayurpankhi boats for Princess Kalabati’s kingdom to win her hand, unaware the princess was unattainable. Buddhu and Bhutum were refused Mayurpankhi Boats for the same journey. The wives mockingly slap Buddhu. Buddhu and Bhutum built boats made of areca-nut sheaths and set sail for Kalabati’s kingdom themselves. Bhutum and Buddhu’s mothers, weeping on the bank, sent small areca-nut boats afloat in hopes that the princes would come home safe.

The princes were captured and eaten by Three Old Crones. Arriving after, Buddhu and Bhutum freed them from the crones’ stomachs through their noses. The princes continued the journey.

The royal boats were then lost in the Red River’s magical, bankless and shoreless waters. Buddhu and Bhutum, in their canoes, guided them to clearer waters where the others revived. Out of greed and cruelty, the princes threw Buddhu and Bhutum overboard.

Because of its magic, the boats suddenly sank. Buddhu dove and found more magic causing the boats to sink with the princes, soldiers and crewmembers into another world. Once he rescurd them he brought the princes, boats and Princess Kalabati back.

After securing the princess the princes once again abandoned Bhutum and Buddhu back in the river as they returned home as heroes.

While visiting their mothers, people were amazed by the magical effects Buddhu and Bhutum’s presense created (market, fruit, and armed guard). The return started the events to restore the unfortunate fourth and youngest queens.

A wedding was arranged between the princess and one of the princes but Princess Kalabati was magically bound to whom had the magical dhol-dogor which Buddhu owned. The prince owners were challenged.

Princess Kalabati and his father the King were restored the fourth and youngest queens to the royal family.

Although Buddhu and Bhutum helped them travel to the kingdom of Princess Kalabati, they shut themselves in to block them from entering.

The Fourth and Youngest Queens discovered the secret of Buddhu and Bhutum's appearance: monkey and owl skins. When those special skins were burned, both princes took their former true appearance as handsome sons of the king.

Buddhu and Bhutum, now known by their new names, Budhkumar and Rupkumar, lived happily as noble princes with their loving wives, the other queens and princes never to be seen again.

A king with seven queens favored the youngest because she was kind. He was childless and sad. When the youngest queen became pregnant, he rejoiced and opened the treasury to the people. The jealous elder queens waited for the birth and falsely signaled the king with a golden chain he'd tied to the youngest queen. Twice they summoned him prematurely. Angered, he threatened to behead them if they did it again before the birth.

The youngest queen bore seven sons and a daughter, but the elder queens hid the children in earthen pots and buried them in an ash heap. They showed the king tadpoles and baby mice, claiming the queen had given birth to those things. The king, enraged, banished the youngest queen, who became a dung-gathering maid.

The kingdom suffered. One day, the gardener found seven Champa and one Parul flower on the ash heap. When he tried to pick them, the Parul flower called to the Champas, who refused to be picked unless the king himself came. Then they refused unless the first queen came, and then the second, and so on. Finally, the flowers said they would only be picked by the dung-gathering maid.

The king brought the youngest queen, and the flowers immediately turned into seven princes and a princess, who embraced their mother. The king saw the truth, buried the wicked queens in a pit of thorns and welcomed his youngest queen and children back to the palace.

Once, a jackal, wanting to be like his father who built a wall, opened a school in the Shanti forest. Insects and other small creatures became his pupils, filling the forest with noise.

A crocodile, not wanting his sons to be uneducated, brought his seven sons to the jackal's school. The jackal promised to make them master archers in a week. Each day, the jackal ate one of the crocodile's sons as a snack.

On the sixth day, the crocodile, excited to see his learned sons, went to the school. The jackal, hiding the last son, convinced the crocodile to leave him for one more day to become a master archer. The foolish crocodile agreed.

The next day, the jackal ate the last crocodile son, closed his school, and fled. The crocodile discovered the truth and vowed revenge.

He hid in a canal, waiting for the jackal. Driven by hunger, the jackal eventually jumped into the canal to catch crabs. The crocodile caught the jackal's leg, but the jackal tricked him into biting a reed instead, and escaped.

Later, the crocodile pretended to be dead on the canal bank. The jackal, wary, said that a dead creature's ears must twitch and tail must slap. The crocodile, trying to prove his death, twitched his head and slapped his tail, revealing himself to nearby cowherds who attacked him. The jackal fled again.

Seeking food, the jackal ate eggplants in a field, where a thorn pierced his nose. He sought help from a barber, who accidentally cut off his nose. The jackal, in exchange for walking away without a further problem, forced the barber to give him his nail-clipper as recompense.

He then traded the nail-clipper for a pot from a potter. The pot was then broken by a firecracker at a wedding. The jackal demanded the bride as compensation.

He left the drummer in charge of the bride, promising to return with a priest. While alone, the bride fell on a knife and split in two. The drummer's wife hid the remains, and the jackal, instead of taking the bride, then took the drummer's drum.

Climbing a palm tree, the jackal played the drum and sang about his misfortunes and gains until a slip caused him to fall.

story_name: the consequence of a broken promise_EN_1
retelling:
The Bengali folktale 'The Consequence of a Broken Promise' is a story that has been passed down through generations, teaching the importance of keeping one's word. Here's a retelling of the tale:

Once upon a time, in a small village in Bengal, there lived a poor farmer named Kalo. Kalo was a hardworking man who tilled the land and grew crops to feed his family. One day, while working in his field, Kalo stumbled upon a hidden treasure buried beneath the earth. Overjoyed by his discovery, he decided to use the treasure to improve his life and the lives of his loved ones.

However, as Kalo was about to leave the field, he heard a voice behind him. It was the voice of the goddess of the land, Dharti Ma. She appeared before Kalo and said, "I have been watching you, Kalo. You are a good man, and I am pleased with your honesty. I will grant you a single wish, but you must promise to use the treasure wisely and never forget the poor and needy."

Kalo, overwhelmed with gratitude, promised to use the treasure to help those in need and to always remember the goddess's kindness. Dharti Ma, satisfied with Kalo's promise, vanished, leaving him to enjoy his newfound wealth.

At first, Kalo kept his promise. He used the treasure to build a new home, feed the hungry, and help the poor. However, as time passed, Kalo began to forget the goddess's words. He became greedy and started to use the treasure only for his own benefit. He built a grand house, bought expensive clothes, and threw lavish parties, but he forgot about the poor and needy.

One day, a severe drought struck the land, and the crops began to wither away. The villagers, including Kalo's family, suffered greatly. Kalo, realizing his mistake, remembered the promise he had made to Dharti Ma. He tried to make amends by helping the poor and needy, but it was too late. The goddess, displeased with Kalo's broken promise, appeared before him once again.

Dharti Ma said, "Kalo, you have forgotten the promise you made to me. You have used the treasure for your own selfish desires, and now you must face the consequences. Your wealth will disappear, and you will be left with nothing."

And so, the treasure vanished, leaving Kalo with nothing but the clothes on his back. The villagers, who had once looked up to Kalo as a generous and kind man, now shunned him. Kalo was left to wander the streets, a poor and broken man, regretting the promise he had broken.

The story of Kalo serves as a reminder of the importance of keeping one's word and the consequences of breaking a promise. It teaches us that our actions have repercussions and that we must always be mindful of the impact our decisions have on others and on ourselves.

What a delightful tale. 'Morar Shakkhi' or 'Witness of the Bubbles' is a traditional Bengali folktale that has been passed down through generations. The story goes like this:

Once upon a time, in a small village, there lived a poor but honest farmer named Morar. He was known for his simplicity, kindness, and truthfulness. One day, while working in his field, Morar noticed a group of bubbles rising from the ground. As he watched, the bubbles grew larger and began to take shape, forming a beautiful, shimmering palace.

Suddenly, a voice boomed from within the palace, "Who is the witness to these bubbles?" Morar, being the only person present, replied, "I am the witness." The voice then declared, "As you are the witness to these bubbles, you will be granted a single wish as a reward."

Morar thought for a moment and then said, "I wish for the ability to help others and bring prosperity to my village." The voice replied, "Your wish is granted, but remember, your kindness and honesty will be the keys to unlocking the true power of this gift."

From that day on, Morar found that he had the ability to make anyone's wishes come true, but only if they were pure of heart and true in their intentions. As news of Morar's gift spread, people from all over the region came to seek his help. Morar, with his newfound power, was able to bring prosperity and happiness to his village, and soon it became a thriving and harmonious community.

However, not everyone who came to Morar was genuine in their intentions. Some people, driven by greed and malice, tried to deceive Morar and exploit his gift for their own gain. But Morar, with his simple and honest nature, was able to see through their deceit and refused to grant their wishes.

One day, a wealthy merchant came to Morar, seeking to become even richer and more powerful. Morar, sensing the merchant's insincere intentions, decided to test him. He told the merchant that he would grant his wish, but only if he could answer a simple question: "What is the most precious thing in the world?"

The merchant, thinking that the answer was wealth or power, replied, "Gold and jewels are the most precious things in the world." Morar smiled and said, "You are mistaken, my friend. The most precious thing in the world is honesty and kindness. As you do not possess these qualities, I will not grant your wish."

The merchant, realizing his mistake, was filled with regret and asked Morar to teach him the value of honesty and kindness. Morar, seeing the merchant's genuine remorse, took him under his wing and taught him the importance of living a simple and truthful life.

And so, Morar's gift continued to bring prosperity and happiness to those who were pure of heart, while also teaching valuable lessons to those who were not. The story of 'Morar Shakkhi' has been passed down through generations, reminding us of the importance of honesty, kindness, and simplicity in our lives.

The tale also highlights the idea that true power and prosperity come not from wealth or material possessions, but from the positive impact we have on the lives of others. Morar's selfless wish and his commitment to helping others ultimately brought him and his community greater joy and fulfillment than any amount of wealth or power could have.

One day, a wicked and powerful demon, named Chand Saudagar, cast a spell on the prince, turning him into a pomegranate (dalim in Bengali). The demon's intention was to keep the prince captive and prevent him from growing up to become a powerful king.

The pomegranate-prince was then sold to a fruit vendor, who took him to a marketplace to sell. A poor old woman, who was a devotee of the goddess Durga, bought the pomegranate, unaware of the prince's true identity.

As the old woman was about to cut the pomegranate, Dalim Kumar, still trapped inside, prayed to the goddess Durga to save him. The goddess, moved by the prince's devotion, appeared before the old woman and revealed the truth about the pomegranate.

Eventually, the pomegranate ripened, and Dalim Kumar emerged from it, restored to his true form as a handsome prince. The old woman, overjoyed, took him to the palace, where he was reunited with his overjoyed parents, the king and queen.

And so, the story of Dalim Kumar, the Pomegranate Prince, has been passed down through generations, reminding us of the power of kindness, devotion, and the protection of the divine.

What a delightful tale! "Shat Bhai Champa" (Seven Brothers and Champa) is a classic Bengali folktale that has been passed down for generations. Here's my retelling of the story:

Once upon a time, in a small village in Bengal, there lived seven brothers who were known for their kindness, bravery, and unwavering dedication to one another. The brothers were extremely close, and their bond was unbreakable. They lived with their mother, who was a wise and loving woman.

One day, while the brothers were out working in the fields, a beautiful and kind-hearted girl named Champa arrived in the village. She was an orphan, and the villagers, taking pity on her, offered her shelter and food. The seven brothers, upon meeting Champa, were immediately drawn to her warmth and generosity. They decided to take her under their wing and treat her like a sister.

As time passed, Champa became an integral part of the brothers' lives. She would help their mother with household chores, cook for the family, and even assist the brothers with their farm work. The brothers, in turn, protected and cared for Champa, making sure she was safe and happy.

However, not everyone in the village was pleased with the brothers' affection towards Champa. The village headman's son, a cruel and power-hungry man named Raghuram, had been eyeing Champa for himself. He began to spread rumors and lies about the brothers, trying to turn the villagers against them.

Raghuram's plan was to marry Champa by force, and he eventually convinced the village headman to arrange the wedding. The seven brothers, determined to protect Champa, came up with a plan to outsmart Raghuram and his father.

On the day of the wedding, the brothers pretended to agree to the marriage, but they had a secret plan in store. As the wedding procession approached Champa's doorstep, the brothers, one by one, created a series of distractions, each one more clever and hilarious than the last.

The first brother, a skilled musician, began to play a mesmerizing tune on his flute, entrancing the wedding party. The second brother, an expert wrestler, challenged Raghuram to a wrestling match, which he easily won. The third brother, a master of disguise, dressed up as a ghost and scared the wedding party, causing them to flee in terror.

The fourth brother, a skilled archer, shot an arrow that severed the rope holding the wedding canopy, causing it to collapse. The fifth brother, a talented cook, prepared a dish so spicy that it made everyone's eyes water, including Raghuram's. The sixth brother, a clever magician, made Raghuram's horse disappear, leaving him to walk to the wedding on foot.

Finally, the seventh brother, the most clever of all, disguised himself as the village priest and performed a fake wedding ceremony, declaring Champa to be the bride of the seven brothers collectively, rather than Raghuram.

The villagers, realizing they had been outsmarted, couldn't help but laugh at the absurdity of it all. Raghuram, humiliated and defeated, slunk away, never to be seen again. The seven brothers, Champa, and their mother lived happily ever after, their bond and cleverness having saved the day.

The story of "Shat Bhai Champa" has been retold and adapted in various forms of Bengali literature, theater, and film, and remains a beloved tale of sibling love, cleverness, and the power of unity in the face of adversity.

'Sheyal Pandit' is a popular Bengali folktale that revolves around the life of a clever and cunning Brahmin named Sheyal Pandit. The story is a testament to the power of wit, intelligence, and cleverness.

Once upon a time, in a small village in Bengal, there lived a poor Brahmin named Sheyal Pandit. Despite his poverty, Sheyal was known for his exceptional intelligence, wit, and cunning nature. He was often called upon by the villagers to settle disputes and offer advice on various matters.

One day, the king of the land announced that he would give his beautiful daughter's hand in marriage to anyone who could answer his three riddles. The king's daughter was renowned for her beauty, and many suitors from far and wide came to try their luck. However, none of them could answer the king's riddles, and they were all sent back disappointed.

Sheyal Pandit, hearing about the king's challenge, decided to take on the task. He set out for the king's palace, despite being poor and not having the means to afford the journey. On his way, he met a group of travelers who were also on their way to the palace to try their luck. Sheyal cleverly joined their group and traveled with them, sharing their food and expenses.

When they arrived at the palace, the king presented his three riddles to Sheyal and the other suitors. The first riddle was: "What is it that is blind, yet sees; silent, yet speaks; and is born, yet dies?" Sheyal thought for a moment and then replied, "The answer is a river. A river is blind, yet it sees the path it flows; it is silent, yet it speaks through the sound of its waters; and it is born, yet it dies when it meets the sea."

The king was impressed with Sheyal's answer and presented the second riddle: "What can be broken, but never held? What can be given, but never sold?" Sheyal thought for a moment and then replied, "The answer is a promise. A promise is something that can be broken, but it can never be physically held in one's hands. A promise is something that can be given, but it can never be sold like a commodity."

The king was even more impressed with Sheyal's answer and presented the third and final riddle: "What is it that goes around the world, yet stays in a corner?" Sheyal thought for a moment and then replied, "The answer is a stamp. A stamp goes around the world on letters and packages, yet it stays in the corner of an envelope or package."

The king was delighted with Sheyal's answers and declared him the winner. As promised, the king gave his beautiful daughter's hand in marriage to Sheyal Pandit. Despite being a poor Brahmin, Sheyal's intelligence, wit, and cunning nature had won him the heart of the princess and the respect of the king.

Sheyal Pandit's story has been passed down for generations in Bengal, and it continues to inspire people to value intelligence, wit, and cleverness. The tale reminds us that with determination and clever thinking, even the poorest and most unlikely person can achieve great things.

story_name: the consequence of a broken promise_EN_3

In the Bengali folktale, "The Consequence of a Broken Promise," a poor farmer promises to offer his most precious possession to the goddess if she blesses him with a bountiful harvest. When his crop flourishes, he reneges on his vow, thinking the goddess won't notice. However, the goddess appears, reminding him of his promise. The farmer tries to deceive her, offering a meager substitute, but she sees through his trickery.

As punishment, the goddess curses the farmer, causing his crops to wither and die. The farmer realizes too late the gravity of breaking his promise. The story teaches the importance of keeping one's word and honoring commitments. It highlights the consequences of dishonesty and the value of integrity. The moral lesson is that breaking a promise can lead to severe repercussions, not just from others, but also from one's own conscience.

The tale also emphasizes the idea that one should not try to deceive or cheat, as it can ultimately lead to one's downfall. The story promotes honesty, trustworthiness, and accountability, encouraging listeners to uphold their promises and respect the trust placed in them. By keeping one's word, individuals can build strong relationships, earn respect, and maintain a clear conscience.

In the Bengali folktale "Morar Shakkhi" or "Witness of the Bubbles," a poor but honest farmer is falsely accused of stealing. The king, determined to uncover the truth, calls upon the farmer to prove his innocence. The farmer, with faith in his own honesty, agrees to undergo a test. He is asked to throw a stone into a river and then retrieve it, but when he does, the stone is not found. The king's men claim the farmer has hidden the stone, further implicating him.

However, the farmer suggests that the bubbles rising from the river be considered as witnesses to his actions. As the bubbles rise and then disappear, the farmer explains that just like the bubbles, the truth will eventually surface. The tale ends with the real thief being caught, and the farmer's innocence being proven.

The moral of "Morar Shakkhi" emphasizes the importance of patience, honesty, and faith in the truth. It teaches that even in the face of adversity and false accusations, one should remain steadfast and have confidence that the truth will ultimately prevail. The story also highlights the value of cleverness and creative thinking in resolving complex situations.

In the Bengali folktale 'Noshi, Dimshi and the Monkey,' two friends, Noshi and Dimshi, befriend a mischievous monkey. The monkey tricks them into giving him their food and belongings, and eventually, they lose everything. The Bengali folktale of 'Khumpui' tells the story of a poor, kind-hearted woman who befriends a magical being. The being, moved by her generosity, grants her a single wish. The Bengali folktale of 'Dalim Kumar' tells the story of a young prince who is born with a pomegranate (dalim) mark on his forehead. story_name: marriage with the prince of snake_EN_4

A long time ago, a couple lived with their beautiful daughter, Bilkis Banu, in a hilly area surrounded by a dense jungle. After the father's death, Bilkis's mother, Sona Banu, became anxious to get her married, but no suitor came forward. One winter morning, a huge python appeared in their courtyard, and the mother and daughter took shelter inside the house, bolting the door. The python lay motionless at the door, and Sona Banu, being greedy and cunning, thought it might be a prince in disguise.

Believing this, Sona Banu decided to marry her daughter to the "Snake Prince." She dressed up Bilkis and sent her to the python, which began to swallow her. As the snake swallowed Bilkis's feet, waist, hands, neck, ears, and head, she cried out in pain, but her mother reassured her that the Snake Prince was putting on golden ornaments. Eventually, the python swallowed Bilkis whole, and Sona Banu waited for the Snake Prince to reveal himself and bring out her daughter, adorned with gold jewelry.

However, the python simply lay motionless, and as night fell, Sona Banu fell asleep. The python digested Bilkis, regurgitated her clothes, and disappeared into the jungle before dawn. When Sona Banu woke up, she found the python and her daughter gone, with only Bilkis's clothes remaining. Realizing her mistake, Sona Banu lamented and wept, finally understanding that the python was not a prince but a real snake. Overcome with grief and loneliness, Sona Banu left her home and took shelter in a populated area, abandoning her house.

story_name: Fifteen Sizzles, Three to Eat, The She-goat's Sign Is By The Binna Tree_EN_4

A husband and wife were arguing while the wife was making pithas. The husband heard the sizzling sound of the pithas 15 times as they were being cooked. She told the neighborhood that her husband was a fortune-teller.

A woman who had lost her goat heard about the husband's supposed abilities and asked for his help. The husband, annoyed at his wife for spreading the rumor, told the woman to return in the afternoon. He then secretly went out and found the goat near a binna tree. When the woman returned, the husband gave her a cryptic message: "15 sizzles, 3 to eat, the she-goat's sign is by the binna tree." Two sisters, Nasi and Dimsi, were walking down a deserted road when they heard a voice calling out to them, asking them to marry. They ignored it at first, but eventually saw a monkey jumping from tree to tree, following them and making proposals. The monkey would offer them gifts, including a water pot, in exchange for marriage. The sisters paid him little attention until they came to a wide canal that they couldn't cross. In exchange for the monkey's help in crossing the canal, they promised to marry him, but after he successfully carried them across, they reneged on their promise, saying they only said it to get across.

The monkey didn't give up and continued to follow them. When the sisters expressed a desire to raise some baby birds from a woodpecker's nest, they again promised to marry the monkey if he could get them the birds. The monkey climbed the tree, but got his hand stuck in the nest while trying to count the chicks and divide them between the sisters. As the sisters waited and grew impatient, the monkey became desperate and tried to pull his hand out, but it was stuck. In a final attempt, he used all his might and managed to tear his arm off, leaving it in the nest, and fell into the mud below, where he became stuck.

In a village called Naran, there lived a priest named Darbasing and his two daughters, Khumpuiti and Khumbarti. Khumpuiti, the elder daughter, was not particularly beautiful, but her younger sister Khumbarti was very beautiful. The family was poor, and the daughters had to work hard in the Jhum fields to survive. One day, while working in the fields, Khumpuiti met a snake who took human form and offered to help them with their work in exchange for food and secrecy. However, the king's other six queens were jealous of Khumbarti and conspired against her, accusing her of giving birth to puppies and kittens instead of human children.

The truth was that Khumbarti had given birth to seven children, six boys and one girl, but the midwives had thrown them into the river and replaced them with animals. The children were found by the river and grew up, and their aunt Khumpuiti, who had become a spirit, guided them to find their mother. The children climbed a banyan tree and were discovered by the king's hunters, who took them to the king. The king was amazed by the children's beauty and ordered all the mothers in the kingdom to try to breastfeed them to find their real mother.

In the end, Khumbarti, who had been mistreated and humiliated by the king and his other queens, was revealed to be the true mother of the children. The king and Khumbarti lived happily ever after with their children.

In a far-off kingdom, a king, queen, and prince lived in a royal palace. The queen's life was tied to a pair of dice, and an ogress, disguised as a beggar woman, tricked the prince into giving her the dice. The ogress then ate the queen and took her form. The prince suspected something was amiss when he saw his "mother" drooling while serving food.

Years passed, and the king had seven more sons. When they grew up, they decided to travel the world. The eldest prince joined them, and they set out on their journey. The ogress-queen, fearing the prince's return, sent a snake named Sutashankha to find out where the prince's life was hidden. The Sutashankha discovered that the prince's life was inside a pomegranate seed, which the ogress then hid beneath the thousand steps of the royal palace.

The seven younger princes arrived at the city of Pashabati, where they were challenged to a game of dice. They lost and were eaten by Pashabati and her sisters. The eldest prince, meanwhile, had become blind and was carried by his winged horse to a city where a princess was eating kings. The prince read a missive found in the snake's belly, which revealed that his brothers had been eaten by an ogress. He decided to rescue them and set out on a journey. He encountered his winged horse, which had turned to stone, and revived it. Together, they crossed treacherous landscapes, including a mountain of cowrie shells and a mountain of bones, to reach the city of Pashabati.

The prince challenged Pashabati to a game of dice and initially lost. However, he brought a kitten that chased away a mouse that was helping Pashabati cheat. The prince then won the game and reclaimed his winged horse. He continued to play and won back his seven brothers, their horses, and Pashabati's kingdom.

Finally, the prince obtained the dice and killed the mouse that was helping Pashabati. The kingdom disappeared, and the prince returned home with his brothers. The queen, who had been in a magical sleep, awoke, and the palace was once again filled with life and celebration. The prince also reunited with the princess from the night-king's land, who brought her entire court and kingdom to join him. The story concluded with the destruction of the palm tree in the royal palace, symbolizing the end of the ogress's evil spell.

Once upon a time, there was a king with seven queens, but none of them had borne him a child, leaving the king and his kingdom in sorrow. One day, a hermit gave the Eldest Queen a tree root, instructing her to grind it and share it among the seven queens, promising that they would bear sons as beautiful as the golden moon.

The queens followed the hermit's instructions, but the Unfavored Queen ate a piece of the root while grinding it, and the Youngest Queen was left with nothing. In the end, the truth was revealed, and the king, realizing his mistake, welcomed the Fourth Queen and the Youngest Queen back to the palace. Buddhu married Princess Kalabati, and Bhutum married Princess Hirabati. The five queens and princes who had wronged them were punished, and the kingdom celebrated the happiness of the king, the two queens, and their sons, Buddhu and Bhutum, who were revealed to be princes in disguise, named Budhkumar and Rupkumar, respectively. The kingdom lived happily ever after.

A king had seven queens, but he loved the youngest one the most because of her gentle nature. The king was sorrowful because he had no children, but his joy was boundless when the youngest queen became pregnant. He announced the news throughout the kingdom and even tied a golden chain to his waist and the youngest queen's, so he could be notified when the child was born.

However, the elder queens were jealous and decided to trick the king. They entered the birthing room and tugged on the chain, pretending the child was born, but when the king arrived, there was nothing. The king took his children and the youngest queen back to the palace, and the kingdom was once again filled with joy and celebration.

---

### **The Marriage with the Prince of Snakes**

Once, in a small village, there lived a kind and beautiful girl named **Champa**. She was the youngest of three sisters, and while her elder sisters were cruel and lazy, Champa was gentle and hardworking.

One day, while fetching water from the pond, Champa saw a **golden snake** floating helplessly in the water. Feeling sorry for it, she carefully picked it up and placed it on the bank. To her surprise, the snake transformed into a **handsome prince**—the **Prince of Snakes**!

The prince thanked her and said, *"You have saved my life. In return, I will marry you."* Before Champa could respond, he disappeared, leaving behind a **golden bangle** as a token of his promise.

When Champa returned home, her sisters were furious. They demanded to know where she had gotten the bangle. When she told them about the snake prince, they mocked her, calling her a liar.

That night, the **Snake Prince** appeared in Champa’s dreams and said, *"Come to the pond at midnight, and I will take you to my palace."* Though frightened, Champa went to the pond as instructed. There, the prince appeared in his true form—a **magnificent serpent**—and took her to his **underwater kingdom**, where he lived in a palace of gold and jewels.

Champa was amazed by the beauty of the snake kingdom. The prince treated her with love and respect, and she lived happily as his queen. However, she missed her family and often thought of her village.

One day, the prince allowed her to visit her home, but he warned her, *"Do not stay past sunset, or you will never return to me."* Champa promised and went to see her sisters.

But her sisters, jealous of her wealth and happiness, tricked her into staying late. When Champa realized the sun was setting, she rushed back to the pond, but it was too late—the prince had vanished, and the pond had dried up.

Heartbroken, Champa wandered the forest, calling for her husband. Finally, an old **sage** appeared and told her, *"The Snake Prince has been cursed. To break the spell, you must find the **magic herb** that grows on the **Mountain of Serpents**."*

With great courage, Champa journeyed to the dangerous mountain, facing many trials. At last, she found the herb and used it to break the curse. The Snake Prince regained his human form permanently, and they returned to his kingdom, where they lived happily ever after.

As for Champa’s cruel sisters, they were turned into **stone statues** as punishment for their deceit.

---

### **Moral of the Story:**
- **Kindness is rewarded**—Champa’s compassion saved the prince.
- **Jealousy leads to ruin**—her sisters’ greed brought them misery.
- **True love conquers all**—Champa’s devotion broke the curse.
